title: Binary search complexity
body: What is the time complexity of binary search on a sorted array of n elements?
explanation: Each comparison halves the search space, so at most ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 comparisons are needed. It requires random access and sorted data.

title: Nested loop complexity
body: What is the time complexity of this code?
explanation: The inner loop runs 0 + 1 + … + (n−1) = n(n−1)/2 times, which is Θ(n²) — constant factors and lower-order terms are dropped.

title: Amortised dynamic array append
body: Why is appending to a dynamic array (List<T>, ArrayList) O(1) amortised?

options.t: Capacity grows geometrically (e.g. doubles), so the occasional O(n) copy is spread over many cheap appends
Each append allocates a new array

answer: Geometric growth makes total copying cost O(n) for n appends.
explanation: Doubling means each element is copied a constant number of times on average. Pre-size the list when the final size is known to avoid reallocations.

title: Pair sum in a sorted array
body: What is the most efficient way to find whether two numbers in a **sorted** array sum to a target?

options.t: Two pointers from both ends moving inward: O(n) time, O(1) space
Sort again then binary search each: O(n² log n)

explanation: If the sum is too small move the left pointer right, if too large move the right pointer left. For unsorted input use a hash set of complements in O(n) time and space.

title: Maximum subarray
body: Which algorithm finds the maximum-sum contiguous subarray in O(n)?
explanation: Track `best = max(best, current = max(x, current + x))` in one pass. Handle all-negative arrays by initialising with the first element.

title: Cycle detection in a linked list
body: How can you detect a cycle in a singly linked list using O(1) extra space?

options.t: Store visited nodes in a hash set
Floyd's tortoise and hare: move one pointer by 1 and another by 2; they meet if there is a cycle

explanation: If fast reaches null there is no cycle. After they meet, resetting one pointer to head and advancing both by one finds the cycle start.

title: Indexed access in a linked list
body: What is the time complexity of accessing the k-th element of a singly linked list?

options.t: O(k), i.e. O(n) in the worst case

answer: O(n) — you must walk from the head.
explanation: Linked lists trade indexed access for O(1) insertion/removal at a known node. Arrays offer O(1) indexing and better cache locality, which often makes them faster in practice.

title: Balanced brackets
body: Which data structure is the natural choice to check whether brackets like `({[]})` are balanced?
explanation: Push opening brackets; on a closing bracket pop and verify it matches. The string is balanced if the stack is empty at the end. O(n) time.

title: BFS data structure
body: Breadth-first search uses which data structure to decide the next node to visit?
explanation: BFS visits nodes level by level, so on unweighted graphs it finds shortest paths in number of edges. Mark nodes visited when enqueued to avoid duplicates.

title: In-order traversal of a BST
body: What order does an in-order traversal of a binary search tree produce?
explanation: In-order visits left subtree, node, right subtree. This property is used to validate BSTs and to find the k-th smallest element.

title: Unbalanced BST worst case
body: What is the worst-case search time in an **unbalanced** binary search tree with n nodes?
answer: O(n) — inserting sorted keys produces a linked-list-shaped tree.
explanation: Self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) guarantee O(log n) height; SortedDictionary/TreeMap use red-black trees.

title: Dijkstra's limitation
body: When does Dijkstra's algorithm fail to find correct shortest paths?

options.t: When some edges have negative weights

explanation: Dijkstra finalises a node when it is popped from the priority queue, assuming distances never decrease later. Use Bellman–Ford for negative weights (it also detects negative cycles).

title: Topological sort
body: Topological sorting is only possible for which kind of graph?
explanation: Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes nodes with in-degree 0; if nodes remain, there is a cycle. Applications: build systems, course prerequisites, task scheduling.

title: Stable O(n log n) sorting
body: Which algorithm is stable **and** guarantees O(n log n) in the worst case?

options.e: Heap sort is O(n log n) but not stable.

explanation: Stability keeps equal keys in their original order — important when sorting by multiple criteria. Merge sort needs O(n) extra space for arrays.

title: Quicksort worst case
body: What is quicksort's worst-case time complexity and when does it occur?

options.t: O(n²), when pivots repeatedly split the array very unevenly (e.g. first-element pivot on sorted input)

explanation: Randomised or median-of-three pivots make this unlikely. Introsort (used by .NET's Array.Sort and C++ std::sort) switches to heap sort when recursion gets too deep.

title: When dynamic programming applies
body: Dynamic programming is applicable when a problem has…
explanation: Divide and conquer (e.g. merge sort) has independent subproblems, so caching gives nothing. Classic DP problems: Fibonacci, knapsack, edit distance, longest common subsequence.

title: Memoisation vs tabulation

options.t: Tabulation is top-down recursion with a cache
Tabulation fills a table bottom-up iteratively; memoisation caches results of top-down recursive calls

answer: Bottom-up table vs top-down cached recursion.
explanation: Tabulation avoids recursion depth limits and often allows rolling-array space optimisation; memoisation computes only the states actually reached.

title: Hash table degradation
body: What makes hash table operations degrade towards O(n)?

options.t: Many keys hashing to the same bucket (poor hash function or adversarial input)

answer: Collisions concentrating keys in few buckets.
explanation: Good hash distribution and resizing keep the load factor low. Mutable keys whose hash changes after insertion become unreachable — make dictionary keys immutable.

title: Fast minimum access
body: Which structure offers O(1) access to the minimum element and O(log n) insertion and removal?
explanation: .NET 6+ provides `PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority>`. Heaps power Dijkstra, scheduling and 'top K' problems.
